author: Jagbir Yadav
text:
🤖 How engineers actually get value from AI — beyond "it writes code for me"

AI in the engineering workflow isn't about replacing the engineer. Used well, it compresses the boring parts and expands what one person can attempt. Used badly, it quietly ships bugs and dulls your skills. Here's the practical split 👇

⚡ Where it lifts productivity (the boring 60%)
• Boilerplate & glue — scaffolding, configs, test stubs, migrations, regex, one-off scripts.
• Reading unfamiliar code — "explain this module," summarize a diff, trace a call path before you touch it.
• Tests & docs — a first pass of unit tests, docstrings, READMEs, commit messages.
• Debugging partner — paste the stack trace, get hypotheses to check (not answers to trust).
• Faster than tab-hunting — API usage, error meanings, "how do I do X in Y."

💡 Where it unlocks innovation (the interesting part)
• Rapid prototyping — stand up a throwaway version in an afternoon to test an idea before committing to it.
• Exploring the option space — ask for 3 different approaches and their trade-offs, then decide.
• Crossing domains — ship a bit of frontend / ML / infra outside your specialty to validate an idea end-to-end.
• Rubber-ducking design — think out loud, pressure-test an architecture, surface edge cases you missed.

✅ How to use it well
• Stay the architect. You own the design, the decisions and the review. AI drafts; you approve.
• Give it real context — the more of your code, constraints and examples it sees, the better the output. This is where agentic tools and MCP shine: they read your actual repo, not a vague prompt.
• Work in small, verifiable steps — diff it, run it, test it. Never merge what you can't explain.
• Treat it like a fast junior — delegate, review, correct. Keep the feedback loop tight.

⚠️ What to be cautious about
• Confident wrong answers — it hallucinates APIs, parameters and "facts." Verify, don't trust.
• Skill atrophy — if you stop understanding what you ship, you can't debug it at 2 a.m. Use AI to learn faster, not to think less.
• Security & IP — don't paste secrets or proprietary code into unapproved tools; know your company's policy.
• Subtle bugs — generated code often looks right and handles only the happy path.
• Over-automation — not everything should be a prompt; sometimes reading the docs is faster and teaches you more.

One line: AI is a force multiplier, not a substitute for judgment. The engineers who win aren't the ones who prompt the most — they're the ones who still understand every line they ship, and use AI to reach further.

## 📍 Session 5: From Linear Regression to ChatGPT — The Evolution of AI, Explained
**#DevOpsToFDE Day 5**

This was the deepest technical session so far — we went from "what even is AI" all the way to why ChatGPT works the way it does. Long post, worth it. 🧵
🔑 **The evolution, step by step:**

**1. AI = Automation.** Traces back to Alan Turing in 1948 and chess automation. The core loop: observe a system → find a pattern → get the benefit.

**2. Expert Systems vs Machine Learning.** Expert systems run on human-coded rules. Machine learning flips that — the system learns patterns from data instead of being told the rules.

**3. Linear Regression = Level 1 ML.** The simplest pattern-finder: y = mx + c. One input, one weight, one output.

**4. Neural Networks = Level 2.** For messier, more complex learning, you scale up: m1x1 + m2x2 + c = y, repeated across layers of neurons. Enough of these neurons stacked together can approximate *any function in the world*. That line alone reframed how I think about "intelligence" as just very well-tuned function approximation.

**5. Function → Probability.** Put a function in front of a large neural network, and instead of a fixed answer, you get a **probability distribution** over possible next outputs.

**6. Gen-AI (LSTM/RNN).** The breakthrough idea: feed the model's own output back into itself, repeatedly, until it hits a stop token. That's literally how an LLM generates a sentence.

**7. The real unlock — "Attention Is All You Need."** Google's landmark research paper solved the problem of *random* word generation by teaching models to relate every word in a sentence to every other word. Attention → coherent sentences → ChatGPT, the first mainstream chatbot built on this architecture.

**8. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation).** Instead of stuffing an entire dataset into a prompt, RAG fetches only the *relevant* slice of data at query time. Efficient and scalable.

**9. From generating text to making decisions.** The next leap: LLMs/agents don't just predict the next word — they call **functions** (generate an image, apply a policy on text, etc.) and make decisions based on outcomes.

**10. Agentic AI, defined properly this time:** a system of AI agents, each playing an individual role, collectively producing one unified decision or output.

Coming from infrastructure, understanding *why* these models behave the way they do — not just how to call an API — feels like finally seeing the engine, not just the dashboard.

I also built a small interactive tool to make this concrete — tokenize a sentence, watch embeddings cluster by meaning, click a word to see its attention weights, then watch next-token prediction happen live. Link in comments 👇

🚀 The first step to building a great ML model isn't training one. It's understanding the data..

Over the last 2 days, I've been deep into Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) on the anonymized SEO and search-performance dataset provided by FlyRank AI as part of the Machine Learning Engineering Internship.

Before writing a single line of modeling code, I wanted to answer one question:
"What is the data actually trying to tell us?"

Here are some of the biggest insights that will shape my upcoming research paper and forecasting model:

🔍 1. The target isn't what I initially assumed
trend_pct measures change in impressions (visibility), not clicks or sessions.
Understanding the target correctly changes how the entire prediction problem should be framed.

📉 2. More than half the content is declining
54.2% → Down
19.9% → Stable
14.6% → Up
7.5% → New
3.8% → Flat
This immediately suggests that content recovery prediction is a more valuable problem than simply identifying growth.

📊 3. What actually predicts growth?
The strongest signals aren't always the obvious ones.
✅ High predictive potential:
Current impressions,Sessions,Clicks,CTR,Content age,Days with impressions
⚠️ Surprisingly weak:
Search volume,Competition,CPC,Word count,Character count
Sometimes the data challenges common assumptions.

🧩 4. Missing values are features, not problems
Some of the most interesting insights came from what wasn't there.
71% missing provider_used → likely an informative "Unknown" category.
26% missing word-count features together → worth creating a missingness indicator.
11.3% missing trend_pct → mostly due to zero previous impressions rather than bad data.
Missing values often tell their own story.

📈 5. Feature redundancy is real
Many variables showed very high Spearman correlations (>0.85).
That means careful feature selection -> or dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA -> will be essential to reduce multicollinearity before modeling.

This phase wasn't just about cleaning a dataset.
It was about discovering how search performance behaves, identifying meaningful signals, and building a stronger foundation for forecasting future content growth and recovery.

🔜 What's next?
I'll be moving beyond the starter dataset and diving into FlyRank AI's Hugging Face data warehouse containing over 82 million rows.
Using DuckDB, I'll be querying and exploring this large-scale dataset to uncover deeper search performance patterns, validate the hypotheses from this EDA, and engineer features that can improve the predictive power of my forecasting model.

Excited to see what insights emerge when working at this scale. 🚀

A big thank you to FlyRank AI for providing such an interesting real-world dataset to explore. Looking forward to the next phase!

Tired of writing the same boilerplate Pandas code for every new dataset? I was too — so I built an AI team to do it for me. 

I'm incredibly excited to open-source MLForge AI — an end-to-end Machine Learning platform that bridges Generative AI, Multi-Agent Orchestration, and classical ML into one unified system.
Instead of jumping between notebooks and spreadsheets, MLForge AI handles the entire lifecycle automatically:

📊 1. Automated EDA: Instantly profiles columns, generates correlation matrices, and detects classification vs. regression tasks.
 
🧹 2. Multi-Agent Cleaning: Autonomous agents catch disguised nulls, handle outliers via IQR, and execute safe imputation—zero manual scripting required. 

⚙️ 3. Feature Engineering: Parses dates, drops zero-variance columns, and automatically applies One-Hot/Label encoding and scaling. 

🤖 4. MLOps & Explainability: Trains multiple algorithms, selects the winner, logs everything to MLflow, and generates SHAP plots so nothing is a black box.

 🧠 5. RAG-Powered AI Assistant: Final reports are chunked, embedded, and stored in a Qdrant vector DB via LlamaIndex. You can ask the built-in chatbot, "What drove the churn model?" and it retrieves the exact answer from its own past work.

🛠 Architecture Under the Hood: Built as a decoupled microservices system using Docker Compose: 🔹 FastAPI & React — Core engine and UI. 🔹 CrewAI & Groq — Specialized agents (Analyst, ML Engineer) reasoning independently via llama-3.1. 🔹 PostgreSQL — Relational backbone for app state. 🔹 Qdrant + LlamaIndex — RAG knowledge layer. 🔹 MLflow — Centralized experiment tracking.

Getting autonomous agents to trigger Python pipelines, log to MLflow, and feed outputs back into a vector DB was an incredible system design challenge.

text:
The difference between someone who uses AI and someone who builds it!
This roadmap is the most honest thing I've seen about what it actually takes to become an AI Engineer.

No shortcuts. No jumping steps. Just 20 levels of compounding knowledge each one building on the last.

Here's what most people get wrong about this path:

They start at Step 15.

They open a LangChain tutorial, copy a RAG pipeline, call an LLM API, and think they're building AI systems. Then something breaks in production and they have no idea why because they skipped the foundation.

The engineers who actually ship reliable AI systems are the ones who:

→ Understand why a model fails, not just that it failed
→ Know when NOT to use an LLM
→ Can debug a data pipeline at 2am
→ Understand the math behind what the model is doing
→ Know the difference between a model that works and a system that works

That depth only comes from taking the steps in order.

Python → Statistics → Data → Classical ML → Deep Learning → Frameworks → NLP → Computer Vision → LLMs → RAG → Agents → MLOps → Production

Each layer earns you the right to work on the next one.

And here's the part the roadmap doesn't show:

At the top of that staircase, what separates good AI engineers from exceptional ones isn't more technical skill.

It's domain knowledge, understanding the problem deeply enough to know what the AI should actually be solving.

For myself in healthcare AI, that means understanding clinical workflows, not just model architectures. In drug discovery, it means understanding molecular biology, not just graph neural networks.

The roadmap gets you to the top.

What you bring from your domain determines what you build when you get there.

🚀 AI/ML Daily 5-Minute Lesson #49
📅 July 16, 2026

Prompt + Retrieved Context

In the previous lesson, we covered metadata in RAG. Today, let’s see how the prompt and retrieved context work together to produce a better answer.

📌 Why This Matters

An LLM needs two things:

• Clear instructions
• Relevant source information

A good prompt tells the model what to do, while retrieved context gives it the evidence needed to answer accurately.

⏰ 5-Minute Concept

Simple workflow:

User Question → Retrieve Relevant Chunks → Add Instructions → Build Prompt → LLM Answer

Example question:

“What should I inspect when Pump 14 has high vibration?”

Retrieved context may include:

• Bearing inspection guidance
• Shaft-alignment steps
• Lubrication checks
• Recent maintenance history

The prompt may say:

“Answer only using the retrieved context. If the answer is not available, say that the information was not found.”

🔑 Key Idea

• The prompt gives instructions.
• Retrieved context provides evidence.
• Both are needed for a useful RAG answer.
• Clear prompts reduce unsupported responses.
• Relevant context improves accuracy.

Remember:

Good Prompt + Relevant Context = Better Answer

🛢️ Oil & Gas / Industrial Example

A technician asks about high vibration on Pump 14.

The RAG system retrieves the correct maintenance-manual sections and adds them to the prompt.

The LLM then creates a focused answer using approved information instead of relying only on its general knowledge.

Business Impact:

✅ More accurate answers
✅ Faster troubleshooting
✅ Fewer unsupported responses
✅ Better use of approved documents
✅ Stronger trust in the AI assistant

🧩 Forward Deployed Engineer Lens

Design prompts around the real user workflow.

Ask:

• What does the technician need?
• Which documents should provide the answer?
• Should the response include steps, risks, or citations?
• What should happen when the context is incomplete?

🚀 Mini Challenge

Write one prompt that tells an LLM to answer a maintenance question using only retrieved manual sections.

🎯 Today’s Goal

✅ Understand prompts and retrieved context
✅ Know how they work together
